        BAR H BAR RANCH AND NATURE PRESERVE’S EXCEPTIONS TO THE
                         PROPOSAL FOR DECISION



        COMES NOW Scimitar Partners LP and Bar H Bar Land & Cattle Co. (collectively, “Bar

H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve” or “ranch”) and files these exceptions to the State Office of

Administrative Hearings’ (“SOAH”) Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) related to Oncor Electric

Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s (“LCRA”)

(collectively, the “Joint Applicants”) proposed 765-kilovolt (“kV”) transmission line from the Bell

Count East Switch to the Big Hill Substation. The deadline to file corrections and exceptions to

the PFD is September 2, 2026, therefore this pleading is timely filed.

   I.      EXCEPTIONS AND CORRECTIONS

        Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve appreciates the work of the SOAH Administrative

Law Judges (“ALJ”) in preparing the PFD and strongly agrees with the PFD’s recommendation to

deny the application for failure of the Joint Applicants to provide adequate notice and that Joint

Applicants failed to establish that that the Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”)

                                                1
 amendment was necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. 1

However, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve disagrees with the PFD’s alternative

recommendation regarding selection of route 894 as the route that should be selected in this

proceeding, should the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission” or “PUCT”) disagree

with the PFD’s recommendation to deny the application.2 Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s

exceptions in this pleading will focus on its disagreement with the alternative recommendation

regarding selection of route 894.

                  A. Routing Criteria (Section VIII)

                           1. Overview of Proposed Routes (Subsection A)

            The PFD in this section identifies which parties support and oppose route 894. 3 However,

the PFD only identifies fourteen parties as opposing selection of route 894, and that list does not

include Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve. 4 Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve states

clearly in its initial brief5 and reply brief6 that it strongly opposes selection of route 894. Further,

without reviewing every single pleading and citing everyone who opposed and supported route

894, it seems highly unlikely in a proceeding that involved hundreds of parties, that only fourteen

parties opposed route 894. In fact, within five minutes of searching counsel for Bar H Bar Ranch

and Nature Preserve found four additional parties in addition to Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve that opposed route 894 and were not included as opposing that route in the PFD. Those

 parties include: K13/K51 Landowners 7; Staten Creek Ranch8; Cherokee Creek Aligned

Intervenors9; and 4K Land and Cattle Company.10 With more time the likelihood of finding

significantly more parties who oppose route 894 is highly likely. This is not a criticism of the

review thousands of pieces of evidence and then draft and file an over 200-page PFD all in 60-

days. This task made it impossible to thoroughly review and identify every party that opposes route

894. This supports the SOAH ALJs’ ultimate recommendation to deny the application given that

insurmountable task. However, to the extent the Commission rejects that recommendations in the

PFD and instead approves the application and selects a route, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve take exception to the representation that only fourteen parties opposed selection of route

894. The number is substantially higher, and that fact should be taken into account when the

Commission decides what route should be selected, to the extent the Commission approves the

application and must select a route.

                           2. Environmental Integrity (Subsection E)

           The PFD does not mention the exotic and endangered species at the Bar H Bar Ranch and

Nature Preserve at all. Further, it does not seem the PFD gives any weight to those endangered

species and the impact that a 765-kV transmission line might have on the animals on the property.

The Bar H Bar Ranch is home to over 30 species of animals including multiple endangered or

 protected animals on the ranch.11 Selection of routes that utilize links H1 or G52, including route

894 supported by Joint Applicants, poses a significant risk to those animals. 12

            These endangered species include at least six species that are listed by either the

International Union for the Conservation of Nature (“IUCN”) or Endangered Species Act (“ESA”)

as protected in some form.13 The below is a list of those protected species and their designation:


                  Species                           Organization                    Protected Status

                                                   IUCN Red List                 Critically Endangered
                  Addax
                                                          ESA                          Endangered

                  Lechwe                           IUCN Red List                    Near Threatened

                                                   IUCN Red List                 Critically Endangered
              Dama Gazelle
                                                          ESA                          Endangered

             Himalayan Tahr                        IUCN Red List                    Near Threatened

                                                   IUCN Red List                       Endangered
              Scimitar Oryx
                                                          ESA                          Endangered




            The Joint Applicants’ did not include any of the above species in their environmental

assessment14 and Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve thinks it is important to show the effects

this oversight would have on these population. To provide examples of the real work effects of

this, the Scimitar Horned Oryx is one of the strongest examples in the world of a species surviving


11

12

 largely because of captive conservation outside its native range. 15 By the 1980s and early 1990s,

the species had effectively disappeared from the wild across its native North African range due to

civil unrest, expanding livestock pressure and habitat degradation. 16 The species was considered

Extinct in the Wild by the IUCN Red List — meaning no self-sustaining wild population remained

in its native habitat.17 At that point, the global survival of the species depended almost entirely on

captive populations held in zoological institutions, private conservation collections and especially

large private ranches in Texas and the American Southwest – like ours. Texas became uniquely

important because private ranches could maintain:


                     very large free-ranging herds,

                     healthy breeding populations,

                     broad genetic diversity,

                     and long-term habitat-scale management that zoos alone often could not provide. 18

            In fact, for many years the majority of the world’s Scimitar-Horned Oryx lived on private

ranches in Texas.19 These ranches effectively became genetic reservoirs, breeding centers and

population insurance against total extinction.20 Without those captive herds, conservation experts

widely acknowledge the species may have been permanently lost. 21 All of this information was

available to Joint Applicants through communications with Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve

 as well as via direct testimony and yet the Joint Applicants did not include this information in their

Environmental Assessment (“EA”) or update their recommendation upon learning about these

species. Further, the PFD ignores this additional evidence because it is not in the EA. Texas has

played a significant role in protecting endangered species from Africa and elsewhere like the

Scimitar-Horned Oryx. Construction of the transmission line on links H1 or G52 will significantly

affect the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s ability to maintain the robust species of animals

it currently has and given that more reasonable options exist to place the transmission line, it does

not make sense to disturb such a large number of endangered and protected species that live on the

ranch.

            Not only does the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve help protect and preserve these

important endangered species, but the ranch itself is an important ecological system that would be

greatly impacted by the construction of links H1 or G52. The goal of the ranch is to create a more

natural ecosystem and reduces the stress and behavioral limitations often associated with heavily

segmented ranch environments.22 Further, the ranch has a highly strategic habitat management

program that includes brush and tree clearing is conducted selectively and with great precision to

create a balanced landscape that supports both grazing and shelter needs. 23 There are open pasture

areas provide adequate forage and movement corridors, while carefully preserved dense tree cover

offers protection from weather, shade during extreme temperatures, and secure areas for birthing

and young animals to remain concealed.24 Water resources are also intentionally distributed

throughout the ranch to promote healthier wildlife patterns and reduce unnecessary competition



22
     Id.
23
     Id.
24

                                                  6
 between species.25 By creating multiple watering locations across the property, animals are able to

spread naturally throughout the landscape rather than concentrating around a single source. 26

            These important environmental conditions, that are carefully maintained by the Bar H Bar

Ranch and Nature Preserve, would be greatly affected by the construction and operation of a

765kV transmission line. In fact, a wide, clear cut transmission corridor would interrupt that

continuity by creating a permanent linear disturbance through the heart of the ranch property. 27

Construction and long-term maintenance of a transmission line would likely require: significant

clearing of trees and brush, creation of possible access roads, heavy equipment activity, long-term

vegetation management (destruction of habitat) and ongoing human presence within previously

undisturbed portions of the ranch.28 These activities would disrupt carefully maintained habitat

areas.29 The corridor itself could also alter wildlife behavior. Many species are sensitive to repeated

disturbance, open utility clearings, vehicle activity, and changes to their environment. 30 Certain

animals may avoid the area altogether, while others could experience increased stress, changes in

movement patterns, or disruptions to breeding behavior and herd structure. 31

            Unfortunately, the PFD does not discuss the environmental impact of the transmission lines

to the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve at all. This is on top of the fact that none of the above,

devastating environmental impacts were captured in the EA nor were they a consideration when

 Joint Applicants recommended route 894. This information should have been considered in the

PFD and given significant weight. Multiple endangered species on the ranch would be affected

and could be significantly harmed if route 894 is selected. This is inconsistent with PURA,

Commission precedent, and good utility practice. To the extent the Commission does approve the

application and adopt a route, the Commission should weigh this additional evidence regarding

the environmental harm to a number of endangered species on the ranch and ultimately select a

route that does not use links H1 or G52.

                           3. Cost (Subsection G)

           The PFD discusses Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserves arguments that the Joint

Applicants significantly undervalued the cost of constructing links H1 and G52 as it relates to

right-of-way (“ROW”) acquisition. However, the PFD instead of doing an analysis of Bar H Bar

Ranch and Nature Preserve’s arguments related to cost, dismisses them stating that “evaluation of

compensation for ROW or condemnation is outside the scope of this proceeding.” 32 The PFD cites

the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order in the docket as supporting its assertion. 33 However,

the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order in no way provides the support for the PFD’s

contention that it alleges it does. The PFD unfortunately conflates two distinct but related issues

regarding compensation for ROW. The Order of Referral and Preliminary Order states that the

question of what is appropriate compensation for ROW or condemnation of property is not to be

addressed in the proceeding.34 The Order of Referral and Preliminary Order further states that

“[t]he Commission does not have the authority to adjudicate or set the amount of compensation



32
     PFD at 130.
33
     Id.
34
     Order of Referral and Preliminary Order at 13 (Mar. 30, 2026).

                                                           8
 for rights-of-way or for condemnation.”35 This is a very narrowly tailored restriction on the

proceeding and is meant to make clear that a party cannot say I am owed “X” for ROW

compensation in this proceeding and then the Commission orders that they are entitled to “X”

payment for ROW compensation. Further, that language in the Order of Referral and Preliminary

Order does not state or imply, as the PFD does, that the Commission cannot consider evidence that

the Joint Applicants have incorrectly assessed ROW costs for the transmission line in a significant

enough manner that the cost analysis is incorrect. If the PFDs reading of the Order of Referral and

Preliminary Order were true, then no party could ever argue that a utility incorrectly assessed cost

as it related to ROW acquisition in any proceeding.

           Instead of accepting the flawed reasoning in the PFD, a more reasonable interpretation of

the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order is that the Commission can consider evidence that the

Joint Applicants severely underestimated ROW acquisition costs without determining the exact

amount of money owned to the landowner. This interpretation allows the Commission to

reasonably review whether cost estimates are accurate while not making a cost determination they

do not have the authority to make. As is evidenced by Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve, the

Joint Applicants underestimated the ROW cost for the ranch by tens of millions of dollars and the

Commission should consider that in selecting a route in this proceeding, should the Commission

reject the PFD’s primary recommendations.

           This is shown by evidence provided by Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve throughout

this proceeding. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve expert witness Michael Noonan provides

in his testimony that the ranch “operations are dependent on pristine habitat, open lands with no




35
     Id.

 interior fences, secluded pastures and water bodies for birthing new animals, and strategic LZs for

aerial helicopter operations used in game management and transfers.” 36 Further, the construction

of links H1 or G52 “would completely inhibit current operations and cause the Bar H Bar Ranch

and Nature Preserve to be unable to continue these specialized operations.” 37 Based upon this loss

of use of the property for its primary function, Mr. Noonan, based on historical appraisal

information of the Ranch, estimates that monetary damages related to the “damages to the

remainder and loss of use on the subject property in the tens of millions of dollars.”38 He further

goes on to state that he saw nowhere in the Joint Applicants’ application that mentions these

extraordinary damages to the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve. 39 Joint Applicant witness

Corin Cooley confirmed this in cross-examination when she admitted that the Joint Applicants did

not do a per link analysis and did not take into account unique features on a property in their cost

analysis.40 Given the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve was not factored into ROW acquisition

for the ranch, the cost of any route, including route 894, that utilizes links H1 or G52 will be

significantly more costly than Joint Applicants have provided in their costs estimates. This is

evidence the Commission should weigh in determining whether route 894 is a more cost-effective

option than other routes. Had this evidence been considered in the PFD it would weigh heavily

against the selection of route 894. We urge the Commission to consider this evidence if it approves

the application and selects a route. In doing so it will become clear that route 894 is not the route

that best meets the routing criteria in PURA.

                            4. Engineering Constraints (Subsection H)

            The PFD does not discuss the helipads at the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve as part

of its discussion of airports and airstrips. 41 We understand that the PFD cannot cover everything

that is discussed as part of the proceeding, but we think that considerations of these helipads is

important in making a routing decision and the PFD failed to identify them in the text of the

recommendation.

            As was highlighted in Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve’s initial brief, the proposed

Link H1 ROW is planned in the areas utilized by the ranch operations and in fact the current link

H1 alignment runs through both LZs and the pristine meadows and water bodies which are critical

to the exotic wildlife operations.42 These LZs would no longer serve a functional purpose in

supporting the legacy exotic wildlife management operations on the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve, or in support of critical medical transport options in case of emergencies if links H1 or

G52 are constructed.43 In fact, given the configuration of the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve

holdings, no helipad sites would be viable or functional post construction of Links G52 and H1,

given the LZ’s would not realistically be able to be located outside of a 5000-foot glide path

guideline. Based upon review of the Kimley-Horn routing study by Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature

Preserve expert witness Michael Noonan, neither of these two primary (2) LZs, which are the only

two LZs which can be used for live animal captures or transfers, have been identified or used as

criteria in identifying a prudent route by Joint Applicants. 44

42

            Further, when asked at hearing why the LZs were constructed the way they were without

any concrete structures and also regarding possible effects of the transmission lines on those LZs,

Mr. Noonan responded that he interviewed both the Hinckley family and the pilot coordinator who

lands the helicopters on the LZs and they explained that the only place the LZs can be placed is

where they currently are.45 He went on to explain the pilot coordinator and family made clear that

the LZs need to be close to the highway to best capture the animals and then de-stress the animals

by loading them quickly.46 Lastly, Mr. Noonan made clear from his conversations with the pilot

coordinator, who does the animal captures for the ranch, that the pilots will not be able to see the

765-kV lines from above, and that if link H1 or G52 were built they would no longer be able to

service the Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve at all.47 So effectively, the LZs can only be

placed where they currently are and if link H1 or G52 were constructed, the pilots who land at the

ranch LZs have stated they no longer could safely land at or use the LZs. This would take away a

vital function of live captures of animals at the ranch and devastate the ranch’s ability to continue

to operate in any meaningful way. Lastly, because these animals are wild, live captures and

transfers near the entrance to the property are vital to protect the safety of the animals and get them

into trailers and on the highway as quickly as possible. There is no other place on the ranch to

safely land and transport the animals via live captures. This should have been addressed in the PFD

and given weight in route selection but was not included. We urge the Commission to give this

evidence weight in making a routing selection.

                            5. Prudent Avoidance (Subsection J)

           The PFD discusses the concept of prudent avoidance and that routing options should try to

avoid population centers and other locations where people gather. 48 Further, the PFD goes on to

assess the number of habitable structures for each proposed route as a part of prudent avoidance. 49

However, it is key to note that the PFD does not modify the number of habitable structures to

account for additional habitable structures identified by landowners including Bar H Bar Ranch

and Nature Preserve. There are at least seven (7) habitable structures currently on the Bar H Bar

Ranch and Nature Preserve, situated in distinct compounds that contain additional habitable

structures utilized frequently. Of these, three (3) primary habitable structures are not shown in Joint

Applicants’ application and are not referenced on the associated mapping or tables contained

therein.50 It is clear the SOAH ALJs did not have the time to include the additional habitable

structures that were identified by Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve and other landowners as

being missing from the assessment done by the Joint Applicants. This failure to include those

additional habitable structures means the PFD relies on outdated information to come to the

conclusion, that should the Commission approve the application, route 894 should be selected.

This furthers the argument that the process did not give the parties or the SOAH ALJs the necessary

time to properly assess what route best meets the criteria outlined in PURA. We urge the

Commission to review this additional information as part of their decision in this proceeding and

urge the Commission not to select route 894.

   II.       CONCLUSION

         As outlined above, Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve agrees with the PFD’s

recommendation to reject the application but disagrees with much of the reasoning in the PFD

regarding its alternative recommendation to select route 894 as the route that best meets the PURA

factors. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve urges the Commission to adopt the PFD’s ultimate

recommendation to reject the application, but to the extent the Commission approves the

application we urge the Commission to reject the PFD and select a route other than route 894 or

any route that utilizes links H1 and G52.

                        3. Cost (Subsection G)

         The PFD discusses Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserves arguments that the Joint

Applicants significantly undervalued the cost of constructing links Hl and G52 as it relates to

right-of-way ("ROW") acquisition. However, the PFD instead of doing an analysis of Bar H Bar

Ranch and Nature Preserve's arguments related to cost, dismisses them stating that "evaluation of

compensation for ROW or condemnation is outside the scope of this proceeding."32 The PFD cites

the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order in the docket as supporting its assertion.33 However,

the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order in no way provides the support for the PFD's

contention that it alleges it does. The PFD unfortunately conflates two distinct but related issues

regarding compensation for ROW The Order of Referral and Preliminary Order states that the

question of what is appropriate compensation for ROW or condemnation of property is not to be

addressed in the proceeding.34 The Order of Referral and Preliminary Order further states that

"[t]he Commission does not have the authority to adjudicate or set the amount of compensation

33 Id.
34 Order of Referral and Preliminary Order at 13 (Mar. 30,2026)

 for rights-of-way or for condemnation."35 This is a very narrowly tailored restriction on the

proceeding and is meant to make clear that a party cannot say I am owed "X" for ROW

compensation in this proceeding and then the Commission orders that they are entitled to "X"

payment for ROW compensation. Further, that language in the Order of Referral and Preliminary

Order does not state or imply, as the PFD does, that the Commission cannot consider evidence that

the Joint Applicants have incorrectly assessed ROW costs for the transmission line in a significant

enough manner that the cost analysis is incorrect. Ifthe PFDs reading of the Order of Referral and

Preliminary Order were true, then no party could ever argue that a utility incorrectly assessed cost

as it related to ROW acquisition in any proceeding.

         Instead of accepting the flawed reasoning in the PFD, a more reasonable interpretation of

the Order of Referral and Preliminary Order is that the Commission can consider evidence that the

Joint Applicants severely underestimated ROW acquisition costs without determining the exact

amount of money owned to the landowner. This interpretation allows the Commission to

reasonably review whether cost estimates are accurate while not making a cost determination they

do not have the authority to make. As is evidenced by Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve, the

Joint Applicants underestimated the ROW cost for the ranch by tens of millions of dollars and the

Commission should consider that in selecting a route in this proceeding, should the Commission

reject the PFD's primary recommendations.

                        5. Prudent Avoidance (Subsection J)

         The PFD discusses the concept of prudent avoidance and that routing options should try to

avoid population centers and other locations where people gather. 48 Further, the PFD goes on to

assess the number of habitable structures for each proposed route as a part of prudent avoidance. 49

However, it is key to note that the PFD does not modify the number of habitable structures to

account for additional habitable structures identified by landowners including Bar H Bar Ranch

and Nature Preserve. There are at least seven (7) habitable structures currently on the Bar H Bar

Ranch and Nature Preserve, situated in distinct compounds that contain additional habitable

structures utilized frequently. Ofthese, three (3) primary habitable structures are not shown in Joint

Applicants' application and are not referenced on the associated mapping or tables contained

therein.50 It is clear the SOAH ALJs did not have the time to include the additional habitable

structures that were identified by Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve and other landowners as

being missing from the assessment done by the Joint Applicants. This failure to include those

additional habitable structures means the PFD relies on outdated information to come to the

conclusion, that should the Commission approve the application, route 894 should be selected.

This furthers the argument that the process did not give the parties or the SOAH ALJs the necessary

time to properly assess what route best meets the criteria outlined in PURA. We urge the

Commission to review this additional information as part of their decision in this proceeding and

urge the Commission not to select route 894.
